title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data acquisition: Udio allegedly used copyrighted sound recordings to train its AI music generation system without obtaining licences from the rights holders. This happened before deployment, at the model-building stage, and affected recordings held by major labels as well as independent artists. The dispute is not limited to a small or incidental sample, as Sony Music alleges the number of affected recordings exceeds 30,000.

The incident shows what happens when a generative AI system is trained on commercially protected material and then released as a product before licensing arrangements are in place. The failure would have been catchable at the data-curation stage, through rights clearance checks before training began. Instead, the legal reckoning came after the system was already in public use, forcing settlements, licensing negotiations, and ongoing litigation as a retrospective correction.

It is not established that Udio acted with intent to infringe, that any court has entered a final finding of liability, or that the damages figures asserted in lawsuits reflect amounts a court will award. Settlements resolve disputes without admissions, and the independent artists' class action and Sony's new lawsuit remain active proceedings whose outcomes are not yet determined.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over copyright infringement. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs, including The Temptations' "My Girl," to train its artificial intelligence system without permission. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs through AI technology. Financial terms were not disclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a major music label and reflects the growing tension between entertainment companies and AI startups over training data. UMG's CEO stated the deal demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies. Udio's CEO expressed enthusiasm about collaborating with UMG to advance AI in music creation. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
